t: Choose K Elements With Maximum Sum
o: For each index i, among indices j with nums1[j] strictly less than nums1[i], report the maximum possible sum of at most k of their nums2 values. Sorting indices by nums1 lets us process values in increasing order: when we reach a group of equal nums1 values, all strictly smaller indices have already been inserted into a data structure maintaining the k largest nums2 values seen so far, and every member of the group shares the same answer. In Example 1, processing 1,2,3,4,5 in order gives answers 0,30,30->wait per group: group 1 answers 0, group 2 answers 30, group 3 answers 80 (top-2 of {20,30,50}), group 4 answers 80, group 5 answers 50.
k: Sort by nums1 and sweep upward; maintain the top-k nums2 values of all strictly smaller elements in a size-k min-heap with running sum.
Equal nums1 values must be answered BEFORE inserting any of them (strict inequality).
Each answer is O(1) after insertion; total O(n log n).

a.i: Order indices by nums1 ascending. Process in groups of equal keys: first assign the current heap-sum as the answer for the whole group, then insert the group's nums2 values into the min-heap, evicting the smallest when size exceeds k and adjusting the running sum.
s: Create an index array sorted by nums1.
Iterate groups of equal nums1; set answer for all group members to the current sum.
Insert group members' nums2 into the heap, popping when size > k and subtracting popped values from the sum.
a.t: O(n log n) for sorting plus O(n log k) heap work
a.sp: O(n) for the order array and heap

w: The critical detail is grouping equal nums1 values and answering before insertion — inserting first breaks strict inequality (Example 2 would wrongly return nonzero). Answers fit in 64-bit (k * 1e6 <= 1e11). Follow-up: if the relation were <= instead of <, you would answer after insertion instead.
